newsitem.title: USA: German upturn on track but needs fuel, officials say.
newsitem.headline: German upturn on track but needs fuel, officials say.

text.p: The German economy appears to have overcome its bout of weakness and is on the path to recovery, German officials said on Saturday.
They warned, however, that investment must pick up if the upturn is to be sustained.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a meeting of top finance officials from the Group of Seven industrial nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- that Europe's economic motor was now clearly headed into recovery.
German growth forecasts of 1.3 percent for 1996 and 2.4 percent for 1997 produced by the International Monetary Fund in a semi-annual report were realistic, he added.
"This meets the expectations of the federal government," Waigel said. "In Germany the pause in growth is over and the upturn has begun."
But Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer warned at a news conference that it was too early to assume that Germany was on a clear, straight path to steady economic growth.

"There are good indications that we are gradually coming into a cyclical upturn," Tietmeyer said. "But the key thing is for investment to pick up. So far that is not the case. That will be decisive for the sustainability of the upturn."
Tietmeyer's words were echoed by Horst Koehler, a former secretary at the German Finance Ministry who is now president of the German savings and clearing banks' association.
"Investment activity is still lagging in Germany," Koehler said in a speech in Washington. "The unblocking of investment must be the central goal of economic policy."
Koehler also called on the Bundesbank to use available room to lower its interest rates to help strengthen recovery.
The German economy, dogged by forecasters' pessimism in the early part of the year, grew at 1.5 percent in the second quarter of the year from the first quarter.
The better than expected figures prompted many economists to raise their forecasts for the full year.

The IMF's 1996 forecast was revised up slightly from a one percent prediction recorded in its last semi-annual report in April. But its 1997 growth estimate, whilst still solid, was revised down slightly from an earlier forecast of 2.9 percent.
But all three officials warned that continued high unemplyment remained a significant problem for the German economy and that steps must be taken to combat this.
The IMF forecast German unemployment of 10.3 percent in 1996 and 10.0 percent in 1997. It called on European countries to take action to deregulate their labour markets.

Waigel, taking note of the comments in the IMF report, pointed to controversial government legislation to help firms' cut costs, noting that this was one step towards helping make Germany more attractive as a production centre.
The minister said in Washington on Friday that he planned to campaign for a cut in the highest rate of income tax to under 40 percent from 53 percent currently on his return to Germany on Monday.
German tax burdens are currently among the heaviest in the industrialised world.
But Koehler, while urging change, nonetheless said it would be a mistake for Germany to adopt wholesale a different economic culture, such as that of the United States.
"I would not advise copying the U.S. model for Germany or Europe," he said. "We should not give up (social consensus) as a German way of solving problems."
